evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

spec.title: BOLD Study: Lyme Borreliosis Diagnostic Delay, Severity Mix, and Antibiotic Duration (6 European Countries, 2021-2022)
spec.boundary: This simulator reproduces only the clinical and treatment-pattern measures the BOLD study reports for medically attended Lyme borreliosis cases in the Czech Republic, Germany, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia, and Sweden (April 2021-December 2022): time to diagnosis by presentation type, hospitalization rate, disseminated-disease proportion, and country-level antibiotic treatment duration. It contains no dollar cost, insurance, caregiving, or productivity-loss data, because the source document reports none.

takeaway.patient: In this European study of 315 enrolled Lyme disease patients (2021-2022), the average time from first symptoms to diagnosis was about 13 days when the only sign was the classic rash (erythema migrans), compared with about 25 days when the infection had already spread beyond the skin (disseminated disease, such as joint, nerve, or heart involvement) - roughly an 11-day gap. Very few patients (about 1%) were hospitalized. The study also found that in Slovakia, far more patients presented with joint involvement rather than the rash than in other countries, for reasons the researchers say they could not pin down to one cause. Typical antibiotic treatment length also varied by country - about 9 days in Slovakia versus about 24 days in Poland - reflecting different national guidelines, not a cost figure.
takeaway.care: Across six European primary-care networks (2021-2022), cases presenting with disseminated disease (spread beyond the inoculation site - e.g., Lyme arthritis, neuroborreliosis, carditis) took about 25 days on average from symptom onset to diagnosis, versus about 13 days for erythema-migrans-only cases, roughly an 11-day gap. Country-level antibiotic treatment duration varied widely (median about 9 days in Slovakia vs. about 24 days in Poland, based on only 8 enrolled Polish cases), reflecting differing national guidelines rather than one standardized protocol. Slovakia's unusually high share of disseminated presentations could not be explained by the study authors, who cite several unresolved possible contributors (strain/co-infection differences, care-seeking behavior, diagnostic or classification practice, rurality, pandemic-related delay) without being able to separate which predominates.
takeaway.policy: In this six-country European surveillance study (BOLD, 2021-2022), 22.8% of 797 medically attended Lyme borreliosis cases had disseminated disease, with large country-to-country variation reported (as low as 1.1% in Slovenia and as high as 78.0% in Slovakia). The authors state this Slovakian pattern may partly reflect several possible factors they could not separate - including diagnostic or classification practice, Borrelia subspecies differences, co-infection, rurality, healthcare-seeking behavior, or pandemic-related care delay - and explicitly cannot isolate which predominates. Mean diagnostic delay was about 25 days for disseminated cases versus about 13 days for erythema-migrans-only cases in the enrolled subset, a roughly 11-day difference. No cost, insurance, or productivity data are reported in this document.

patient: If you or a family member is being evaluated for Lyme disease, consider asking your clinician whether the type of presentation (rash-only versus signs the infection has spread) affects how quickly a diagnosis is usually reached, since this study found spread-beyond-skin cases took longer to diagnose on average.

If prescribed antibiotics, you might ask what course length is typical where you are treated, since this study found typical durations ranged from about 9 to 24 days across the six countries studied, reflecting different national guidelines rather than a single standard.

Note that very few patients in this specific study (about 1%) were hospitalized; this may be useful context to raise in conversation with a clinician, though it describes this particular European sample and not a guarantee for any individual case.
care: The diagnostic-delay gap between disseminated and erythema-migrans-only presentations may be worth checking against your own practice's intake and triage workflow for atypical, non-rash presentations.
Consider whether antibiotic course-length practice at your site aligns with your national guideline or diverges from it, given the wide country-level range this study observed.

The low hospitalization rate (about 1%) observed in this outpatient-focused cohort may inform expectations about primary-care-based management capacity, recognizing this reflects a specific European sample.
Given that 5.4% of antibiotic-treated cases in this study required more than one course, a structured follow-up check for non-responders may be worth reviewing.
policy: The disseminated-disease proportion and its country variation could be used as an epidemiological input for vaccine-impact or disease-burden modeling, while keeping the unresolved, multi-factor explanation for Slovakia's outlier pattern clearly flagged rather than attributed to any single cause.
A linked costing study (direct medical, non-medical, and productivity-loss) for this same cohort could be commissioned or supported, since this document reports none.
The systemic surveillance gap the authors describe (EU-level neuroborreliosis surveillance only began in 2018) is worth noting when evaluating cross-country manifestation-frequency comparisons.

Before generalizing diagnostic-delay or treatment figures to the full 797-case population, consider the documented difference between enrolled and unenrolled cases (enrolled cases skew older, more female, and more disseminated).

inputs.label: Mean diagnostic delay, disseminated-disease cases

inputs.interpretation: This is the study's observed mean days from symptom onset to diagnosis for patients with disseminated disease (signs beyond the original tick-bite site). Moving it changes the diagnostic delay gap output; raising it explores how a longer delay for spread disease would widen the gap this study reported.

inputs.label: Hospitalization rate among enrolled cases
inputs.source: Section 3.5, p.8 (4/315 enrolled cases). A 0-5 percent range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's observed share of the 315 enrolled cases who were hospitalized. Moving it shows how the hospitalization output below would look at illustrative alternate values within a plausible range around the study's own low observed figure.

inputs.label: Disseminated-disease proportion, all medically attended cases
inputs.source: Abstract; Section 3.2, p.4 (182/797 medically attended cases). A 0-80 percent range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source, chosen to span the country-level variation (1.1 to 78.0 percent) the document itself reports.
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's observed share of all 797 medically attended cases with disseminated disease rather than erythema migrans alone. Moving it illustrates how the disseminated-proportion output below would differ across the wide country-level range the study reports, without identifying a single cause for that variation.

inputs.label: Median antibiotic treatment duration, Slovakia
inputs.source: Table 2, pp.9-10 (n=100 enrolled Slovakian cases). A 5-15 day range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source, chosen to stay below the Poland duration input's range.
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's reported median (typical) antibiotic treatment duration in Slovakia, the shortest of the six countries studied. Moving it changes the antibiotic duration gap output; lowering it further widens the gap between Poland's and Slovakia's typical course lengths.

inputs.label: Median antibiotic treatment duration, Poland
inputs.source: Table 2, pp.9-10 (n=8 enrolled Polish cases). A 16-30 day range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source, chosen to stay above the Slovakia duration input's range so the study's reported ordering cannot be reversed by exploration.
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's reported median antibiotic treatment duration in Poland, the longest of the six countries studied, based on a small sample of 8 enrolled cases. Moving it tests how sensitive the country duration gap output is to this small-sample figure.

outputs.label: Diagnostic delay gap, disseminated minus EM-only (positive = disseminated diagnosed later)
outputs.interpretation: This is the gap between the study's observed mean time to diagnosis for disseminated-disease cases and for erythema-migrans-only cases in the enrolled BOLD cohort. A positive value means disseminated cases were, on average, diagnosed later than EM-only cases in this study; the document's own figures (24.9 vs. 13.4 days) show about an 11-day gap, and the input ranges here are set so this ordering cannot be reversed by exploration.

outputs.label: Antibiotic duration gap, Poland minus Slovakia (positive = Poland's typical course longer)
outputs.interpretation: This is the gap between the typical (median) antibiotic treatment duration reported for Poland and for Slovakia, the longest and shortest country-level medians in the study. A positive value means Poland's typical course was longer than Slovakia's in this study; this reflects differing national prescribing guidelines rather than a cost figure, and Poland's figure rests on only 8 enrolled cases.

outputs.label: Hospitalization rate, enrolled cases
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of the 315 enrolled BOLD cases who were hospitalized (4 of 315 in the study). A higher value would mean more cases required inpatient care; the study's own figure is low, consistent with Lyme borreliosis being managed mostly in outpatient primary-care settings in this cohort.

outputs.label: Disseminated-disease proportion, all medically attended cases
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of all 797 medically attended BOLD cases (a broader group than the enrolled subset) with disseminated disease rather than the rash alone. A higher value means more of the medically attended population had the more severe, spread form of disease; the document reports wide country-to-country variation here that its authors say they cannot fully explain.

## BOLD Study Simulator — Parameters and Sources

This simulator reproduces clinical and treatment-pattern measures from the BOLD (Burden of Lyme Disease) study, a prospective surveillance study across 14 primary-care practices in Lyme-endemic regions of the Czech Republic, Germany, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia, and Sweden, April 2021-December 2022 (n=797 medically attended cases; n=315 enrolled for detailed follow-up).

**Inputs.** Diagnostic delay for erythema-migrans-only and disseminated cases are observed mean days from symptom onset to clinical diagnosis in the enrolled cohort (Section 3.4, p.8; Table S4). Exploration ranges were chosen so each input stays on its own side of the other (EM-only 5-20 days; disseminated 21-35 days), preserving the study's own reported ordering (disseminated cases took longer, about 24.9 vs. 13.4 days) through any sensitivity exploration. Hospitalization rate (1.3%, 4/315 enrolled cases; Section 3.5, p.8) and disseminated-disease proportion (22.8%, 182/797 medically attended cases; Abstract; Section 3.2, p.4) are observed point estimates with assumed exploration ranges noted on each input. Antibiotic treatment duration (median days, not mean) in Slovakia (9 days, n=100) and Poland (23.5 days, n=8) are the shortest and longest country-level medians reported (Table 2, pp.9-10); these reflect country prescribing guidelines, not a standardized protocol or any cost figure. Ranges were set so Poland's stays above Slovakia's, preserving the reported ordering.

**Outputs** compute simple gaps (disseminated minus EM-only delay; Poland minus Slovakia duration, with sign conventions stated in each label) and pass through the hospitalization and disseminated-proportion figures unchanged.

**Limitations.** This document reports no direct medical, non-medical, or indirect (productivity or caregiving) cost data anywhere, so no dollar outputs are included here. The disseminated-disease proportion varies sharply by country (1.1% in Slovenia to 78.0% in Slovakia, per the document); the authors state this may partly reflect several unresolved, unseparated factors (Borrelia strain or co-infection differences, healthcare-seeking behavior, diagnostic or classification practice, rurality, pandemic-related delay) and explicitly cannot isolate which predominates - this simulator's country-level inputs do not resolve that question. The enrolled subset (n=315) differs systematically from the 482 unenrolled cases (older, more female, more disseminated disease), so these figures should not be generalized to all 797 cases. The overall mean diagnostic-delay figure (16.5 days, not separately modeled here) has not been checked in this document for variation by sex, age, or race/ethnicity; federal survey data such as NHIS and BRFSS generally supports such disaggregated analysis even though this European study did not perform it. Separately, the authors describe a systemic evidence-system limitation: EU-level standardized surveillance for at least one manifestation (neuroborreliosis) only began in 2018, limiting prior cross-country comparability and motivating BOLD's own harmonized case-definition approach. Patient-reported outcomes, laboratory-testing practices, and post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome findings from this same cohort are deferred to separate manuscripts not available here.

spec.title: BOLD Study: Lyme Borreliosis Diagnostic Delay, Severity Mix, and Antibiotic Duration (6 European Countries, 2021-2022)
spec.boundary: This simulator reproduces only the clinical and treatment-pattern measures the BOLD study reports for medically attended Lyme borreliosis cases in the Czech Republic, Germany, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia, and Sweden (April 2021-December 2022): time to diagnosis by presentation type, hospitalization rate, disseminated-disease proportion, and country-level antibiotic treatment duration. It contains no dollar cost, insurance, caregiving, or productivity-loss data, because the source document reports none.

takeaway.patient: In this European study of 315 enrolled Lyme disease patients (2021-2022), the average time from first symptoms to diagnosis was about 13 days when the only sign was the classic rash (erythema migrans), compared with about 25 days when the infection had already spread beyond the skin (disseminated disease, such as joint, nerve, or heart involvement) - roughly an 11-day gap. Very few patients (about 1%) were hospitalized. The study also found that in Slovakia, far more patients presented with joint involvement rather than the rash than in other countries, for reasons the researchers say they could not pin down to one cause. Typical antibiotic treatment length also varied by country - about 9 days in Slovakia versus about 24 days in Poland - reflecting different national guidelines, not a cost figure.
takeaway.care: Across six European primary-care networks (2021-2022), cases presenting with disseminated disease (spread beyond the inoculation site - e.g., Lyme arthritis, neuroborreliosis, carditis) took about 25 days on average from symptom onset to diagnosis, versus about 13 days for erythema-migrans-only cases, roughly an 11-day gap. Country-level antibiotic treatment duration varied widely (median about 9 days in Slovakia vs. about 24 days in Poland, based on only 8 enrolled Polish cases), reflecting differing national guidelines rather than one standardized protocol. Slovakia's unusually high share of disseminated presentations could not be explained by the study authors, who cite several unresolved possible contributors (strain/co-infection differences, care-seeking behavior, diagnostic or classification practice, rurality, pandemic-related delay) without being able to separate which predominates.
takeaway.policy: In this six-country European surveillance study (BOLD, 2021-2022), 22.8% of 797 medically attended Lyme borreliosis cases had disseminated disease, with large country-to-country variation reported (as low as 1.1% in Slovenia and as high as 78.0% in Slovakia). The authors state this Slovakian pattern may partly reflect several possible factors they could not separate - including diagnostic or classification practice, Borrelia subspecies differences, co-infection, rurality, healthcare-seeking behavior, or pandemic-related care delay - and explicitly cannot isolate which predominates. Mean diagnostic delay was about 25 days for disseminated cases versus about 13 days for erythema-migrans-only cases in the enrolled subset, a roughly 11-day difference. No cost, insurance, or productivity data are reported in this document.

patient: If you or a family member is being evaluated for Lyme disease, consider asking your clinician whether the type of presentation (rash-only versus signs the infection has spread) affects how quickly a diagnosis is usually reached, since this study found spread-beyond-skin cases took longer to diagnose on average.

If prescribed antibiotics, you might ask what course length is typical where you are treated, since this study found typical durations ranged from about 9 to 24 days across the six countries studied, reflecting different national guidelines rather than a single standard.

Note that very few patients in this specific study (about 1%) were hospitalized; this may be useful context to raise in conversation with a clinician, though it describes this particular European sample and not a guarantee for any individual case.
care: The diagnostic-delay gap between disseminated and erythema-migrans-only presentations may be worth checking against your own practice's intake and triage workflow for atypical, non-rash presentations.
Consider whether antibiotic course-length practice at your site aligns with your national guideline or diverges from it, given the wide country-level range this study observed.

The low hospitalization rate (about 1%) observed in this outpatient-focused cohort may inform expectations about primary-care-based management capacity, recognizing this reflects a specific European sample.
Given that 5.4% of antibiotic-treated cases in this study required more than one course, a structured follow-up check for non-responders may be worth reviewing.
policy: The disseminated-disease proportion and its country variation could be used as an epidemiological input for vaccine-impact or disease-burden modeling, while keeping the unresolved, multi-factor explanation for Slovakia's outlier pattern clearly flagged rather than attributed to any single cause.
A linked costing study (direct medical, non-medical, and productivity-loss) for this same cohort could be commissioned or supported, since this document reports none.
The systemic surveillance gap the authors describe (EU-level neuroborreliosis surveillance only began in 2018) is worth noting when evaluating cross-country manifestation-frequency comparisons.

Before generalizing diagnostic-delay or treatment figures to the full 797-case population, consider the documented difference between enrolled and unenrolled cases (enrolled cases skew older, more female, and more disseminated).

inputs.label: Mean diagnostic delay, erythema-migrans-only cases
inputs.source: Section 3.4, p.8; Table S4. A 5-20 day range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source, chosen to stay below the disseminated-delay input's range.
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's observed mean days from symptom onset to diagnosis for patients whose only sign was the erythema migrans rash. Moving it changes the diagnostic delay gap output below; lowering it explores how much larger the gap would be if EM-only diagnosis were faster relative to disseminated cases.

inputs.label: Mean diagnostic delay, disseminated-disease cases
inputs.source: Section 3.4, p.8; Table S4. A 21-35 day range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source, chosen to stay above the EM-only delay input's range so the ordering the study reports cannot be reversed by exploration.
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's observed mean days from symptom onset to diagnosis for patients with disseminated disease (signs beyond the original tick-bite site). Moving it changes the diagnostic delay gap output; raising it explores how a longer delay for spread disease would widen the gap this study reported.

inputs.label: Hospitalization rate among enrolled cases
inputs.source: Section 3.5, p.8 (4/315 enrolled cases). A 0-5 percent range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's observed share of the 315 enrolled cases who were hospitalized. Moving it shows how the hospitalization output below would look at illustrative alternate values within a plausible range around the study's own low observed figure.

inputs.label: Disseminated-disease proportion, all medically attended cases
inputs.source: Abstract; Section 3.2, p.4 (182/797 medically attended cases). A 0-80 percent range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source, chosen to span the country-level variation (1.1 to 78.0 percent) the document itself reports.
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's observed share of all 797 medically attended cases with disseminated disease rather than erythema migrans alone. Moving it illustrates how the disseminated-proportion output below would differ across the wide country-level range the study reports, without identifying a single cause for that variation.

inputs.label: Median antibiotic treatment duration, Slovakia
inputs.source: Table 2, pp.9-10 (n=100 enrolled Slovakian cases). A 5-15 day range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source, chosen to stay below the Poland duration input's range.
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's reported median (typical) antibiotic treatment duration in Slovakia, the shortest of the six countries studied. Moving it changes the antibiotic duration gap output; lowering it further widens the gap between Poland's and Slovakia's typical course lengths.

inputs.label: Median antibiotic treatment duration, Poland
inputs.source: Table 2, pp.9-10 (n=8 enrolled Polish cases). A 16-30 day range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source, chosen to stay above the Slovakia duration input's range so the study's reported ordering cannot be reversed by exploration.
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's reported median antibiotic treatment duration in Poland, the longest of the six countries studied, based on a small sample of 8 enrolled cases. Moving it tests how sensitive the country duration gap output is to this small-sample figure.

outputs.label: Diagnostic delay gap, disseminated minus EM-only (positive = disseminated diagnosed later)
outputs.interpretation: This is the gap between the study's observed mean time to diagnosis for disseminated-disease cases and for erythema-migrans-only cases in the enrolled BOLD cohort. A positive value means disseminated cases were, on average, diagnosed later than EM-only cases in this study; the document's own figures (24.9 vs. 13.4 days) show about an 11-day gap, and the input ranges here are set so this ordering cannot be reversed by exploration.

outputs.label: Antibiotic duration gap, Poland minus Slovakia (positive = Poland's typical course longer)
outputs.interpretation: This is the gap between the typical (median) antibiotic treatment duration reported for Poland and for Slovakia, the longest and shortest country-level medians in the study. A positive value means Poland's typical course was longer than Slovakia's in this study; this reflects differing national prescribing guidelines rather than a cost figure, and Poland's figure rests on only 8 enrolled cases.

outputs.label: Hospitalization rate, enrolled cases
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of the 315 enrolled BOLD cases who were hospitalized (4 of 315 in the study). A higher value would mean more cases required inpatient care; the study's own figure is low, consistent with Lyme borreliosis being managed mostly in outpatient primary-care settings in this cohort.

outputs.label: Disseminated-disease proportion, all medically attended cases
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of all 797 medically attended BOLD cases (a broader group than the enrolled subset) with disseminated disease rather than the rash alone. A higher value means more of the medically attended population had the more severe, spread form of disease; the document reports wide country-to-country variation here that its authors say they cannot fully explain.

scenarios.label: Slovakia's disseminated-disease share
scenarios.goal: See how much the disseminated-disease rate varies by country versus the pooled EU figure.
scenarios.description: Replaces the pooled six-country disseminated-disease proportion (22.8%) with Slovakia's own reported country-level proportion (78.0%), illustrating country-to-country variation the authors caution against pooling into one EU rate.

scenarios.label: Slovenia's disseminated-disease share
scenarios.goal: See the opposite extreme of country variation in disseminated-disease presentation.
scenarios.description: Replaces the pooled six-country disseminated-disease proportion (22.8%) with Slovenia's own reported country-level proportion (1.1%), the lowest among the six BOLD countries.

scenarios.label: EU overall median vs Poland
scenarios.goal: Tests whether Poland's long course looks as extreme against the EU median as against Slovakia's short course.
scenarios.description: Substitutes the study's overall six-country median antibiotic duration (11 days) for Slovakia's country-specific median (9 days), narrowing the comparison baseline used against Poland's reported 23.5-day median.
